results.question: Do creatures phasing back in trigger enter the battlefield abilities?
results.text:
No. Creatures that phase in do not cause enters-the-battlefield abilities to trigger.

Definition of phasing: Phasing is a static ability that modifies the untap step; during the untap step phased-in permanents with phasing phase out and phased-out permanents that phased out under a player’s control phase in (they become “phased in”) (see rule 702.26a). A phasing event is not a zone change: the permanent isn’t considered to have left and re-entered the battlefield, tokens continue to exist while phased out, and zone-change triggers don’t trigger when a permanent phases in or out (see rules 702.26d and 702.26c).

Why enters-the-battlefield abilities don’t trigger: Enters-the-battlefield abilities are zone-change triggers (see rules 603.6a and 603.6c). Because phasing is not a zone change and the rules explicitly state that zone-change triggers don’t trigger when a permanent phases in or out, a creature phasing in doesn’t trigger enters-the-battlefield abilities (see rule 702.26d). The only related exception in the provided rules is that abilities that trigger when a permanent phases out are checked “looking back in time” for the phase-out event (see rule 603.10b); that exception applies to phase-out triggers, not phase-in/enters-the-battlefield triggers.

This ruling is the same in multiplayer and two-player games; nothing in the provided rules makes phasing-in cause ETB triggers in multiplayer.

Assumption about timing: This answer assumes the usual phasing actions (phasing in happens as part of the untap-step turn-based action). If a card’s own text or an explicit ruling (not provided here) said otherwise, follow that card text (card text overrides general rules).

results.question: how does trample work with deathtouch?
results.text:
Direct answer: A creature with trample that has deathtouch only needs to assign one point of damage to each blocking creature (or whatever minimum is lethal taking into account damage already marked and other simultaneous assignments); after assigning that lethal amount to each blocker, any remaining damage can be assigned to the defending player or planeswalker per trample. 

Why: Define the terms first. Deathtouch means any nonzero amount of damage dealt by that source is considered lethal for determining excess damage (a single point counts as lethal) [702.2c]. Trample is a static ability that changes how an attacking creature assigns combat damage: the controller assigns damage to blocking creatures first and, once those blockers have been assigned lethal damage, may assign any excess to the defending player or planeswalker [702.19a],[702.19b]. When calculating how much is “lethal” for assignment and how much is excess, use the rules for excess-damage calculation; because of deathtouch, any amount greater than 1 is excess damage when the source has deathtouch, so only 1 damage need be assigned to each blocker before assigning excess to the player/planeswalker [120.4a].

Important details and interactions: 
- When checking how much must be assigned to be lethal, take into account damage already marked on the blocking creature and damage from other creatures being assigned during the same combat damage step; do not take into account effects that would change the amount of damage actually dealt (for example, prevention or changes that only affect what is dealt) [702.19b].
- Damage marked on creatures remains until the cleanup step, so such damage counts toward lethal for assignment and state-based checks [120.6].
- After combat damage is dealt, a creature that was dealt damage by a source with deathtouch is destroyed as a state-based action (if its toughness is greater than 0) [704.5h].

Example: A 6/6 attacker with trample and deathtouch blocked by a single 2/2 must have 1 damage assigned to that 2/2 (that 1 is “lethal” because of deathtouch); the remaining 5 damage may be assigned to the defending player [702.19b],[702.2c],[120.4a].

results.question: is storm a triggered ability that can be countered?
results.text:
Yes. “Storm” is a triggered ability that functions on the stack, and that triggered ability can be countered only by effects that specifically counter abilities (not by effects that only counter spells).

Definition: A triggered ability is an ability written like “When/Whenever/At [trigger event], [effect].” It triggers when its trigger event occurs (603.1; 603.2a). Storm is a triggered ability that functions on the stack and reads, in part, “When you cast this spell, copy it for each other spell that was cast before it this turn...” (702.40a). When you cast a spell with storm, the storm ability triggers and is put on the stack the next time a player would receive priority (603.3). Abilities on the stack are not spells, so they can’t be countered by effects that counter only spells; they can instead be countered by effects that specifically counter abilities (113.9).

Assumption about timing: This answer assumes the usual sequence where you cast a spell with storm, the storm ability triggers, and that triggered ability is put on the stack (603.2a; 603.3). If you meant whether the copies the storm ability makes can be countered: those copies are copies of the original spell created by the storm triggered ability when it resolves (702.40a); whether those copies can be countered depends on whether they’re spells on the stack and on what effects target them (113.9).

results.question: can i use cards with hybrid mana symbols in a commander deck that only has one of those colors?
results.text:
No — only if every color present in the card’s hybrid mana symbol(s) is also in your commander’s color identity. A hybrid mana symbol counts as all of its component colors, so a {R/G} symbol makes that card both red and green (and therefore it’s only legal in a commander deck whose commander’s color identity includes both red and green), while a monocolored hybrid symbol such as {2/R} counts as red only (so that card is legal in a red commander deck) (see rules [107.4e], [903.4], [903.4f]). 

Definitions and reasoning:
- Color identity: the color or colors of any mana symbols in a card’s mana cost or rules text (plus color indicators or characteristic-defining abilities). That is what determines whether a card can be included in a commander deck (see rules [903.4], [903.4f]).
- Hybrid mana symbol: a mana symbol that represents a cost that can be paid in one of two ways; a hybrid mana symbol is considered to be all of its component colors (see rule [107.4e]).

Examples: Wort, the Raidmother’s color identity is red and green, so a card with a {R/G} cost is legal in a Wort, the Raidmother deck because its color identity is red and green; a card with a {G/W} cost is not legal in a Wort, the Raidmother deck because that card’s color identity would include white, which Wort, the Raidmother’s color identity does not include (see rule [903.5c] and [107.4e]).

Also note: mana symbols that appear in a card’s rules text count toward its color identity, too, so hybrid symbols in rules text likewise affect legality (see rule [903.4]).

results.question: can I respond to the untap step?
results.text:
No — you cannot respond during the untap step. No player receives priority during the untap step, so you may not cast spells or activate abilities until the next time a player would receive priority (usually the upkeep) (see rules [502.4] and [117.3a]).

Definitions and key points (so the answer stands on its own):
- Priority: which player may take actions such as casting spells or activating abilities. The player with priority may act; if no player has priority, no one may act (see rule [117.1] and [117.3a]).
- Phasing: a static ability that modifies the untap step. During the untap step, all phased-in permanents with phasing that the active player controls phase out, and all phased-out permanents that phased out under that player’s control phase in; this happens immediately when the untap step begins and doesn’t use the stack (see rules [702.26a] and [502.1]). If an effect causes a player to skip their untap step, the phasing event doesn’t occur that turn (see rule [702.26m]).

Why you can’t respond: the untap step consists of turn-based actions (phasing, the day/night check if relevant, then choosing and untapping permanents), and those actions don’t use the stack and happen while no player has priority (see rules [703.4a], [703.4c], [502.3], [502.2]). A step in which no players receive priority ends only when those specified actions are complete (see rule [500.3]). Any abilities that trigger during the untap step are held until the next time a player would receive priority and will be put onto the stack at the beginning of the upkeep before the active player receives priority (see rules [502.4] and [503.1a]).

Short practical summary: you can’t cast spells or activate abilities during the untap step itself; wait until the triggered abilities from the untap (if any) are put on the stack at the start of the upkeep or until the active player actually receives priority after the untap/upkeep actions are finished.

results.question: are creatures still considered attacking creatures during the end of combat step?
results.text: Yes. Creatures are still attacking creatures during the end of combat step; they remain attacking until they’re removed from combat or the combat phase ends, and the combat phase doesn’t end until the end of combat step ends. Definition: an attacking creature is “a creature that has either been declared as part of a legal attack during the combat phase (once all costs to attack, if any, have been paid), or a creature that has been put onto the battlefield attacking. It remains an attacking creature until it’s removed from combat or the combat phase ends, whichever comes first” ([508.1k]). Reasoning: the end of combat step is part of the combat phase, so creatures that were attacking remain attacking during that step because they only stop being attacking when removed from combat or when the combat phase ends ([508.1k], [506.4]). Effects that trigger “at end of combat” do so as the end of combat step begins, and effects that last “until end of combat” do not expire at the start of the end of combat step but instead expire when the combat phase ends ([511.2], [500.5a]). As soon as the end of combat step ends, the combat phase ends and all creatures are removed from combat ([511.3]), at which point they cease to be attacking creatures ([506.4]).

results.question: Do you cast lands?
results.text: No. You do not cast lands; you play lands. To play a land means to put that land onto the battlefield as a special action (this is not casting a spell). Playing a land is a special action that doesn’t use the stack, the land is never a spell, and players can’t respond to the act of playing a land with instants or activated abilities. You may play a land only while you have priority during a main phase of your turn when the stack is empty and you haven’t already played a land this turn; you can’t play a land on someone else’s turn. An effect that “puts” a land onto the battlefield is not the same as playing a land and doesn’t count as the land you played this turn. A card that is both a land and another card type (for example, an artifact land) can only be played as a land and can’t be cast as a spell. Also note that lands normally have no mana cost and are played without paying costs, so there is nothing to cast for them.

results.question: if a card loses all abilities, does that include keyword abilities?
results.text:
Yes — keyword abilities are abilities, so an effect that makes an object “lose all abilities” removes its keyword abilities (for example, flying, trample, deathtouch, etc.).

Definitions and reasoning:
- A “keyword” is an ability; keyword abilities are abilities an object can have (see rule 702.1 and 702.1d). 
- Effects can add or remove abilities; an effect that makes an object lose abilities removes those abilities (see rule 113.10). 
- Effects that say an object “can’t have” an ability remove that ability and also prevent that ability from being added later (see rule 113.11). 
- Ability-adding and ability-removing effects (including keyword abilities and keyword counters) are applied in layer 6 when determining an object’s characteristics (see rule 613.1f). That is where a “lose all abilities” effect removes keyword abilities. 
- An ability sticker grants abilities to an object; those granted abilities are still abilities subject to removal (see rule 123.7a). 

Important exception (not covered by “lose all abilities”): if an effect doesn’t grant an ability but instead sets a characteristic or states a quality of an object, that isn’t an ability and so wouldn’t be removed by an effect that only makes the object “lose all abilities.” Examples: effects that say a permanent “is red” or that a permanent “can’t be blocked” are treated as a characteristic or a stated quality rather than a granted ability (see rule 113.12). Also note that “This creature can’t block” is itself an ability (see rule 113.2a), which is distinct from the phrase “can’t be blocked” used as an example of a stated quality in rule 113.12.

results.question: can i draw cards if i'm already at my maximum hand size?
results.text: Yes. Being at your maximum hand size does not stop you from drawing cards; maximum hand size only matters during your cleanup step when you must discard down to that size. Definition of key terms: “Maximum hand size” — each player’s maximum hand size is the number of cards they’re allowed to keep in hand; as part of the cleanup step, the player must discard excess cards down to that number [402.2]. “Draw a card” — drawing is an action that happens one card at a time when instructed [121.2]. Reasoning: the rules that define maximum hand size and the discard that enforces it do so as a turn-based action during the cleanup step and do not say that drawing is prohibited at other times; instead, when the cleanup step begins the active player discards down to their maximum hand size immediately (a turn-based action that doesn’t use the stack) [514.1, 703.4n, 402.2]. Because nothing in those rules says a player can’t draw while at or above their maximum hand size, you may draw cards; if you still have more than your maximum as your cleanup step begins, you then discard down to the maximum as required [514.1, 703.4n, 402.2]. Also note that cards are drawn one at a time when instructed to draw multiple cards [121.2].

results.question: what happens when a planeswalker has 0 or less loyalty counters?
results.text:
If a planeswalker has 0 loyalty counters, that planeswalker is put into its owner’s graveyard as a state-based action. State-based actions happen automatically whenever their conditions are met and don’t use the stack. The rules provided speak specifically about the 0-loyalty case (they say “0”), and they don’t describe a separate rule for “less than 0.” In play, damage and other effects can remove loyalty counters (damage to a planeswalker removes that many loyalty counters), and once the planeswalker’s loyalty is 0 a state-based action puts that planeswalker into its owner’s graveyard.

results.question: do non-creature artifacts die?
results.text:
No — a non‑creature artifact on the battlefield does not “die.” The game’s defined term dies means “is put into a graveyard from the battlefield,” and that term applies only to creatures and planeswalkers ([700.4]).

Explanation and how this applies:
- Dies means “is put into a graveyard from the battlefield” for a creature or planeswalker only ([700.4]). Saying a permanent “dies” is therefore only correct for creatures and planeswalkers. 
- A noncreature permanent (including a noncreature artifact) has no power or toughness while it’s a noncreature permanent ([208.3]), so the state‑based actions that put creatures with 0 or less toughness into their owners’ graveyards ([704.5f]) or that destroy creatures that have been dealt lethal damage ([704.5g]) don’t apply to noncreature artifacts. 
- A permanent (of any type) can still be put into its owner’s graveyard from the battlefield for other reasons, or an effect that literally uses the word “destroy” can destroy it; the rule defining destroy says the only ways a permanent can be destroyed are effects that use the word “destroy” or the creature‑specific state‑based lethal/deathtouch checks, and that if a permanent is put into its owner’s graveyard for any other reason it hasn’t been “destroyed” ([701.8b]).
- If an object is both an artifact and a creature (for example, an artifact creature), it is a creature as well as an artifact and so can “die” ([300.2]).

Summary action guidance: If a noncreature artifact is put into a graveyard from the battlefield, you should not say it “dies”; call it “was put into its owner’s graveyard” or “was destroyed” only if an effect specifically destroyed it using the word “destroy.”

results.question: what happens if i should draw a card when my library is empty?
results.text: You lose the game the next time a player would receive priority if you attempt to draw a card while your library is empty; that loss is handled as a state-based action. Reasoning and definitions: - Draw: “To put the top card of a player’s library into their hand” (a draw is a turn-based action or an effect that uses the word “draw”) [Draw][121.1]. - What happens when you try to draw with an empty library: If a player attempts to draw a card from a library with no cards in it, that player loses the game the next time a player would receive priority (this is a state-based action) [121.4][704.5b][704.1]. - Replacement effects that replace draws are applied even if no cards could be drawn; such a replacement effect still applies when a draw is attempted from an empty library [121.6a][614.11]. - If an effect merely offers a choice to draw when the library is empty, the player may choose to do so (unless another effect says that player can’t draw cards) [121.3][121.3a]. - If an effect moves cards from a library to a hand without using the word “draw,” those cards weren’t drawn (so draw-triggered abilities and draw-replacement effects do not apply, and the empty-library draw-loss rule does not apply to those moves) [121.5]. - If an effect requires drawing more cards than remain in the library, the player draws as many as possible and then loses the game the next time a player would receive priority (drawing the remaining cards, then the loss occurs) [104.3c][609.3].

results.question: what are the steps in combat and when do I have priority as the defending player?
results.text:
Direct answer: The combat phase has five steps — beginning of combat, declare attackers, declare blockers, combat damage, and end of combat (see rule 506.1). As the defending player you have priority whenever the game gives you priority (see definition below), except during turn‑based actions that don’t use the stack (you can’t cast spells or activate abilities while those turn‑based actions are being performed).

Details and when you don’t have priority:
- The five combat steps are: beginning of combat; declare attackers; declare blockers; combat damage; end of combat (506.1). Declare blockers and the combat damage step are skipped if no creatures are attacking (506.1).
- Beginning of combat: immediately after the beginning of combat step begins, the active player chooses a defending player as a turn‑based action; that choice doesn’t use the stack (507.1, 703.4h, 506.2a). You do not get to cast spells or activate abilities while that turn‑based action is being taken.
- Declare blockers: the defending player declares blockers as a turn‑based action immediately after the declare blockers step begins; that turn‑based action doesn’t use the stack (509.1, 703.4j). The declaration itself is not a point at which spells or abilities can be cast or activated.
- Combat damage: first, attackers assign combat damage and then blockers assign combat damage; those assignments are turn‑based actions (510.1, 703.4k). Second, all assigned combat damage is dealt simultaneously; no player gets to cast spells or activate abilities between assignment and the dealing of damage (510.2). Note there can be two combat damage steps if creatures have first strike or double strike (506.1).
- End of combat: as soon as the end of combat step begins, the active player gets priority (511.1), so the defending player does not automatically have priority at that instant.
- Two‑player vs multiplayer: in a two‑player game the nonactive player is the defending player (506.2). In multiplayer the defending player(s) may be chosen or may be all opponents depending on the multiplayer option in use (507.1, 802.2); combat damage assignment in multiplayer follows APNAP order (802.5).

Definition of the key term “priority”: priority is the right to take actions; the player with priority may cast spells, activate abilities, and take special actions (117.1). When a turn‑based action “doesn’t use the stack,” it is performed without giving players priority to cast spells or activate abilities during that action (see the turn‑based action rules cited above).

Assumption: I’m assuming you mean when, during the combat phase, the defending player may cast spells or activate abilities. If you meant a different question about timing (for example, during a specific triggered ability), say so and give the exact timing you care about.

results.question: can i respond to a mana ability?
results.text:
No — you can’t respond to a mana ability. "Respond" means to cast an instant or activate an ability while another spell or ability is on the stack (that is, to act “in response” to it) [Respond], [117.7]. A mana ability doesn’t go on the stack and instead resolves immediately when it’s activated or when it’s triggered, so there is no opportunity to put a spell or ability on the stack in response [605.3b], [605.4a], [405.6c].

Definitions and important details:
- "Mana ability": an activated ability that doesn’t require a target, could add mana when it resolves, and isn’t a loyalty ability (or a triggered ability that meets the triggered-mana criteria) [605.1a]. An ability remains a mana ability even if the game state prevents it from producing mana [605.2].
- Activated mana abilities can be activated in some situations where you don’t have priority (for example, while casting a spell or paying a cost), but they still resolve immediately and can’t be responded to [605.3a], [605.3b].
- Triggered mana abilities resolve immediately after the mana ability that triggered them, without waiting for priority [605.4a].
- If an ability has a target, it is not a mana ability and follows normal rules for activated or triggered abilities (and thus can be responded to) [605.5a].
- If a player had priority before a mana ability was activated, that player gets priority after it resolves; you must wait until after resolution to act [405.6c].

results.question: can you explain layers?
results.text:
Layers are the step-by-step system the game uses to determine how continuous effects change an object’s characteristics: start with the object’s printed (or created) characteristics, then apply applicable continuous effects in a fixed series of layers and sublayers, using timestamps (or dependency when relevant) to order effects within a layer; the game continually and automatically applies those effects and the resulting changes are instantaneous. 

Definitions and core points
- Layer: the ordered group in which certain kinds of continuous effects are applied (see rule 613.1 and the Layer heading). [613.1]
- Continuous effect: an effect that changes an object’s characteristics over time and is applied by the layer system; the application of continuous effects is continually and automatically performed by the game and their results are instantaneous. [613.5]
- Starting values: begin with the object’s actual characteristics printed on the card, or for a token or copy the values that defined it when it was created. Then apply effects in the layer sequence. [613.1] 
- Commonly referenced layers (examples in the provided rules):
  - Layer 1: effects that modify copiable values (including a sublayer 1a for copiable effects such as copy effects). [613.1a] [613.2a]
  - Layer 3: text-changing effects (see also the definition of text-changing effect). [613.1c] [612.1]
  - Layer 4: type-changing effects (card types, subtypes, supertypes). [613.1d]
  - Layer 5: color-changing effects. [613.1e]
  - Layer 7: power-and-toughness effects (applied in sublayers, e.g. setting vs. modifying P/T). [613.4] [613.5]

Ordering within and across layers
- Layers are applied in the fixed numerical order (1 through 7 as appropriate). Start with the object’s printed values, then apply all applicable effects in layer order. [613.1]
- Within a given layer or sublayer, effects are usually applied in timestamp order: earlier timestamps apply before later ones. [613.7]
- Some layers have sublayers and specify how those sublayers are applied; within each sublayer, timestamp order is used unless dependency applies. [613.2] [613.4]
- Dependency: if a dependency exists between two continuous effects in the same layer or sublayer, that dependency overrides timestamp order when determining which applies first. [613.8] [Dependency]

Multi-part effects and persistence
- If a single effect has parts that apply in different layers, each part applies in its appropriate layer. If an effect starts applying to a particular set of objects in one layer, it will continue to apply to that same set of objects when its other parts are applied in later layers, even if the ability generating the effect is removed during the process. Examples in the rules include an effect that both changes color (layer 5) and gives +1/+1 (layer 7c), and Act of Treason’s “gain control” (layer 2) then “it gains haste” (layer 6). [613.6]

What this means in practice (examples from the rules)
- The application is automatic and instantaneous: Honor of the Pure’s effect and a color-changing effect interact so a creature can gain and lose the +1/+1 as its color changes (example using Honor of the Pure). A +1/+1 counter and an until-end-of-turn +4/+4 spell stack and then an enchantment that gives +0/+2 applies, showing how multiple P/T effects combine in layer 7 sublayers (examples using Gray Ogre and Honor of the Pure). [613.5]
- Type-, color-, and P/T-setting effects applied to the same permanent are handled in their respective layers; Svogthos, the Restless Tomb’s example shows a land becoming a creature (layer 4), a color change (layer 5), and a P/T-setting effect (layer 7b) all being applied in the proper order. [613.6]

Quick procedure to determine an object’s current characteristics
1. Start with the object’s printed (or created) characteristics. [613.1]
2. Apply continuous effects in numerical layer order (1 → 2 → 3 → 4 → 5 → 6 → 7), honoring sublayer ordering where specified. [613.1] [613.2] [613.4]
3. Within each layer or sublayer, apply effects in timestamp order unless a dependency exists between effects, in which case dependency overrides timestamp order. [613.7] [613.8]
4. Remember that multi-part effects apply their parts in the appropriate layers and remain applied to the same set of objects across those layers even if their source is removed during application. [613.6]
