results.question: how does the legend rule work?
results.text:
Direct answer: The legend rule is a state-based action that says if a player controls two or more legendary permanents with the same name, that player chooses one of them and the rest are put into their owners’ graveyards.

Explanation and key definitions:
- “Legend rule” / what happens: As a state-based action, when two or more legendary permanents with the same name are controlled by the same player, that player chooses one to keep and the rest are put into their owners’ graveyards. (See 704.5j and Legend Rule.)
- “Legendary” / “legendary permanent”: “Legendary” is a supertype normally relevant on permanents; any permanent with the supertype “legendary” is subject to the state-based action described by the legend rule. (See Legendary and 205.4d.)
- Tokens with names: If an effect creates a legendary token by naming it (for example, “create [name], a …”), that token has that name and is a legendary permanent for this purpose, so it is included by the legend rule. (See 111.9.)
- Supertypes don’t change with type changes: An object’s supertypes (including legendary) are independent of its card types or subtypes; if an object becomes or stops being a certain card type, it keeps any supertypes it has (so a land that is legendary remains legendary). This is relevant when effects change types while leaving the legendary supertype in place. (See 205.4b.)
- Planeswalkers and older prints: Planeswalker cards printed before the planeswalker-uniqueness rule was removed were given the legendary supertype and thus are subject to the legend rule like other legendary permanents. (See 306.4.)

How this applies in play: The check and the putting-into-graveyard action are state-based and are applied automatically; the rule text’s phrasing (“that player chooses one of them, and the rest are put into their owners’ graveyards”) makes clear the choice is that player’s to make. This applies independently for each player (the rule speaks about the player who controls two or more such permanents). (See 704.5j.)

results.question: when does my creature die after its been marked with a lethal amount of damage?
results.text:
Your creature is destroyed the next time state-based actions are checked after the lethal damage is marked; state-based actions will destroy it because its marked damage is greater than or equal to its toughness. (If a regeneration effect replaces that event, the creature isn’t destroyed then — see below.)

Definitions and short explanation
- Lethal damage: an amount of damage greater than or equal to a creature’s toughness (see “Lethal Damage”). [Lethal Damage]
- State-based actions: game actions that happen automatically whenever certain conditions are met; they don’t use the stack and can destroy a creature when it has been dealt lethal damage. [704.1]

Why and when this happens
- Damage dealt to a creature is marked on it; that marked damage remains until the cleanup step. [302.7] [120.6]
- Damage being dealt is processed into its results (the step in which damage becomes marked and its results are handled). [120.4c]
- Damage itself does not directly “destroy” a creature; instead, if the total damage marked on a creature is greater than or equal to its toughness, that creature has been dealt lethal damage and is destroyed as a state-based action. [120.5] [704.5g]
- State-based actions are checked and performed automatically before a player would receive priority. In practice, that means as soon as the game next checks state-based actions after the damage is marked (for example, immediately after damage is dealt and before any player receives priority), the creature will be destroyed. [117.5] [117.2d]
- Damage marked on permanents is only removed during the cleanup step (or if the permanent regenerates). If the creature regenerates in response, regeneration can replace the destruction event. [514.2] [704.5g]

Timing note (assumption clarification)
- The answer assumes the damage has already been dealt and marked on the creature. If the damage is still being processed (for example, during the damage-dealing event), that processing step completes first (see 120.4c), and then state-based actions are checked. [120.4c]

results.question: can I cast my commander from exile?
results.text:
No — you can’t cast your commander from exile by default. You may only cast it from exile if a specific rule or effect explicitly allows you to cast that card from exile; otherwise you (or the game) will typically move that commander into the command zone and you can cast it from there.

Reasoning and relevant rules (summary):
- “Cast” (definition): To cast a spell is to take it from where it is, put it on the stack, and pay its costs; casting includes the steps of proposing the spell and determining and paying costs. See rules 601.2b and 601.2f for the full procedure and constraints on casting.
- Commander-specific baseline: A commander is a card designated as that deck’s commander in any zone, and effects that refer to casting a commander refer to a spell that is a commander (rule 903.3d). A commander may be cast from the command zone; a commander cast from the command zone costs an additional {2} for each previous time it was cast from the command zone that game (the “commander tax”) (rule 903.8).
- Exile to command-zone interaction: If a commander is in exile and it was put there since the last time state-based actions were checked, its owner may put that commander into the command zone as a state-based action (rule 903.9a). That means the owner can choose to have the commander moved to the command zone and then cast it from the command zone under rule 903.8 rather than attempting to cast it from exile.
- Casting from exile is otherwise allowed only by specific effects: Some effects explicitly allow a player to cast spells from exile (rule 601.3f). The rules text includes examples of specific card types/abilities that allow casting from exile (for example, plotted cards per rule 702.170d or Adventure cards that are exiled per rule 715.3d). Exiled cards are face up by default and may be examined (rule 406.3b), which can be relevant when a specific effect says to cast a spell from exile.

Putting that together: unless an effect explicitly lets you cast that commander from exile (601.3f and any specific rule that grants that permission, e.g., 702.170d or 715.3d), you may instead have it put into the command zone via the commander return-to-command-zone state-based action (903.9a) and then cast it from the command zone (903.8). If no such effect exists and you don’t move it to the command zone, you cannot legally begin casting it from exile under the general casting rules (601.2b, 601.2f).

If you want a definitive ruling for a specific card or effect, state the card or the exact effect text; some card effects explicitly let you cast from exile and would change this answer.

results.question: what happens during the cleanup step?
results.text: During the cleanup step: first the active player discards down to their maximum hand size if necessary, then all damage is removed from permanents and all “until end of turn” and “this turn” effects end. Normally no player gets priority during the cleanup step, but the game checks state-based actions and whether any triggered abilities are waiting; if state-based actions are performed and/or triggered abilities are waiting, those state-based actions are performed, those triggered abilities are put onto the stack, and then the active player gets priority (otherwise the step ends with no priority). See details below.

results.question: when are state-based actions checked?
results.text: State-based actions are checked whenever the game would give a player priority — in other words, throughout the game each time a player would get priority the game checks for and performs all applicable state-based actions before that player actually receives priority. State-based actions are game actions that happen automatically whenever certain conditions are met and they don’t use the stack. When checked, all applicable state-based actions are performed simultaneously as a single event; if any are performed the check is repeated, then any triggered abilities waiting to be put on the stack are put on the stack, and the process repeats until no state-based actions are performed and no triggered abilities are waiting, after which the appropriate player gets priority. Turn-based actions that occur at the beginning of a step or phase are dealt with first (before state-based actions are checked). Normally no player gets priority during the cleanup step, but if state-based actions would be performed or triggered abilities are waiting, those state-based actions are performed and then triggered abilities are put on the stack and the active player gets priority.

results.question: when can I concede a game?
results.text: You may concede the game at any time; if you concede you immediately leave that game and lose it. Definition: to concede means to quit the game — conceding causes that player to leave the game immediately and lose the game (see rule 104.3a). You may concede even if another player currently controls you (see rule 723.6), and you may concede at times that aren’t using the stack (see rule 405.6g). Card text cannot override the fact that a player can concede at any time; conceding at any time is the exception noted in rule 101.1 (see rules 101.1 and 104.3a). In Two-Headed Giant, if a player concedes their team leaves the game immediately and that team loses the game (see rule 810.8b).

results.question: how do I know who the active player is?
results.text:
The active player is the player whose turn it is. [102.1]

Definition: “Active player” means the player whose turn it is; that player is the one referred to by the term unless a card or effect says otherwise. [102.1]

How you use that in play:
- In a two-player game, the nonactive player is simply the other player; during combat the active player is the attacking player and the nonactive player is the defending player. [102.1] [506.2]
- If multiple players are making choices or taking actions at the same time (for example, a spell or effect says “each player” does something), the active player makes any required choices first, then the next player in turn order, and so on (the Active Player, Nonactive Player or APNAP ordering). After those choices are made, the actions happen simultaneously. [101.4]
- Priority (who may cast spells, activate abilities, etc.) goes to the active player when priority is being determined. [117.1] [508.2]
- In games using the shared team turns option, the team whose turn it is is the active team; references to “active player” in abilities that could apply to more than one active player are resolved so that the ability refers to one specific active player chosen when the effect is applied. [805.4a] [805.9]

If you want to know who is the active player at any moment, check whose turn it is; that player is the active player. [102.1] If you need to know who decides first when several players choose or act simultaneously, use the APNAP order (active player first). [101.4]

results.question: when someone other than the active player casts a spell, who gets priority first?
results.text:
Direct answer: The player who cast the spell (the nonactive player in this case) gets priority immediately afterward — the caster keeps priority after casting (I’m assuming you mean “after the spell is cast”).

Reasoning and definitions: ‘‘Priority’’ is the game rule that determines who may take actions such as casting spells or activating abilities (rule 117.1). If a player has priority when they cast a spell, that same player receives priority afterward (rule 117.3c). If the spell was cast in response to another spell or ability, that new spell will resolve first, but the player who cast it still receives priority right after casting (rule 117.7). By contrast, after a spell or ability resolves, the active player receives priority (rule 117.3b).

Multiplayer note: This explanation applies regardless of number of players; if a spell’s casting instructs opponents to make choices at the same time the spell is being cast, rule 601.7 and 601.7b explain when those opponents make those choices relative to the caster, and rule 101.4 (APNAP) governs the order of simultaneous choices when it applies.

If you meant a different timing (for example, who has priority right after the spell resolves rather than right after it’s cast), say so and I’ll answer that specific moment.

results.question: when the active player cast a spell, who gets priority first?
results.text:
The player who cast the spell gets priority immediately afterward. 

Definition of “priority”: Priority is the system that determines who may cast spells, activate abilities, and take special actions; the player with priority may take those actions. (See rule 117.1.)

Reasoning: If a player has priority when they cast a spell, that player receives priority afterward, so the caster receives priority immediately after casting. (See rule 117.3c.)

Clarification: If you instead meant “who gets priority after the spell resolves,” the active player receives priority after a spell or ability resolves. (See rule 117.3b.)

results.question: can I hold priority to cast more spells after I've cast one or more spells?
results.text:
Yes. If you had priority when you cast a spell, you receive priority afterward and may cast additional spells (you can repeat this while you keep having priority before casting each one).

Definition — priority: Priority is the game state that determines which player may cast spells, activate abilities, and take special actions at a given time (see rule [117.1]).

Why: Rule [117.3c] says that if a player has priority when they cast a spell, that player receives priority afterward; rule [601.2i] reiterates that if the spell’s controller had priority before casting it, they get priority after it’s cast. If you cast a spell while another object is already on the stack, that new spell is considered cast “in response to” the earlier one and will resolve first ([117.7]).

Exception: If you cast a spell because an effect specifically instructs or allows you to cast it while another object is resolving (that is, you’re casting it during resolution), no player receives priority after it’s cast, so you cannot “hold” priority in that situation ([608.2g]).

Additional note: A phase or step with priority only ends when the stack is empty and all players pass in succession, so players do get further opportunities to add spells or actions before that phase or step ends ([500.2]).

results.question: when are lore counters put on sagas?
results.text:
Lore counters are put on Sagas in two ways: (1) as replacement effects when a Saga enters the battlefield (some Sagas enter with one or a chosen number of lore counters), and (2) as a turn-based action immediately after a player’s precombat main phase begins, when that active player puts a lore counter on each Saga they control that has one or more chapter abilities. 

Definition: A lore counter is a counter Sagas use to track their progress (Sagas use lore counters to track their progress). Replacement-entry: Each Saga without read ahead has the intrinsic ability “This Saga enters with a lore counter on it,” and each Saga with read ahead has the intrinsic ability to choose a number of lore counters as it enters; those are replacement effects that cause the Saga to enter the battlefield with the indicated lore counters. Turn-based placement: Immediately after the active player’s precombat main phase begins, that active player puts a lore counter on each Saga they control with one or more chapter abilities; this is a turn-based action that doesn’t use the stack. 

Additional note: “Active player” means each player performs this action on their own precombat main phase (i.e., when they are the active player).

results.question: what is a delayed triggered ability?
results.text:
A delayed triggered ability is an ability that was created by a spell, ability, replacement effect, or similar effect as that effect resolved (or as a static ability allowed a player to take an action) that contains “when,” “whenever,” or “at” and does something later instead of immediately. It is created during resolution or when a replacement/static effect is applied and won’t trigger until it has actually been created. 

Key points and definitions
- Creation: A delayed triggered ability is created during the resolution of spells or abilities, as the result of a replacement effect being applied, or when a static ability lets a player take an action. (Creation rules: 603.7, 603.7a, 603.7f, 603.7g.)
- Wording: A delayed triggered ability will contain “when,” “whenever,” or “at.” (603.7, 603.7a.)
- Timing of trigger: The delayed triggered ability won’t trigger until it has been created; if the event that would trigger it already happened before creation, it won’t trigger for that past event. (603.7a.)
- How often it triggers: A delayed triggered ability triggers only once—the next time its trigger event occurs—unless it has a stated duration (for example, “this turn”). If its trigger event happens more than once simultaneously and there is no stated duration, the controller of the delayed triggered ability chooses which event causes it to trigger. (603.7b.)
- Refexive triggered abilities: A resolving spell or ability can create a delayed triggered ability that’s checked immediately after creation and triggers based on whether the trigger event occurred earlier during that resolution (a reflexive delayed triggered ability). (603.12.)
- References to objects and zones: A delayed triggered ability that refers to a particular object still affects that object even if it changes characteristics, but it does nothing if the object is no longer in the zone the ability expects when the delayed triggered ability resolves; if the object left the zone and later returned, it’s a new object and won’t be affected. (603.7c; see 400.7.)
- Source and controller: If a spell creates a delayed triggered ability, the source of that delayed triggered ability is that spell and its controller is the player who controlled that spell as it resolved. If an activated or triggered ability creates a delayed triggered ability, its source and controller follow that creating ability. If a static ability’s replacement effect creates the delayed triggered ability, the source is the object with that static ability and the controller is the same as that object’s controller when the replacement was applied. (603.7d, 603.7e, 603.7f.)
- Special cases: If an activated or triggered ability creates a delayed triggered ability that triggers when that creating ability has resolved a certain number of times in a turn, the delayed triggered ability is created only once at the appropriate resolution. (603.7h.) Also, if a permanent spell resolving has a static ability that functions on the stack and creates a delayed triggered ability, that delayed triggered ability is created as the permanent is put onto the battlefield. (608.3g.)
- X values: If a delayed triggered ability refers to X and X was chosen as part of the cost of the spell or ability that created the delayed triggered ability, the delayed triggered ability uses the same X value. (107.3n.)

results.question: can non-permanent spells have abilities?
results.text: Yes. Non-permanent spells (instant and sorcery spells on the stack) can have abilities. Any text on an instant or sorcery is a spell ability that is followed as instructions while that instant or sorcery spell is resolving, except when that text is instead an activated ability, a triggered ability, or a static ability that fits the criteria in rule 113.6; abilities of an instant or sorcery usually function only while that object is on the stack. An “ability” is a characteristic an object has that lets it affect the game or an activated/triggered ability on the stack (i.e., abilities can be spell abilities or activated/triggered abilities). Also note that activated and triggered abilities on the stack aren’t spells. (See rules 113.3a; 113.6; 113.1a; 113.1c; 113.9.)

results.question: can I use a mana ability when a spell with split-second is on the stack?
results.text:
Yes. You can activate mana abilities while a spell with split second is on the stack. Split second is defined as “As long as this spell is on the stack, players can’t cast other spells or activate abilities that aren’t mana abilities” [702.61a], and the rules explicitly state that players may activate mana abilities while a spell with split second is on the stack [702.61b].

A “mana ability” is an activated or triggered ability that meets the criteria for mana abilities (see rule 605.1) and is treated specially by the rules [113.4]. Mana abilities don’t use the stack and resolve immediately when activated (they can’t be targeted or countered) [605.3b], and if a player had priority before a mana ability was activated they get priority after it resolves [405.6c]. Players may activate mana abilities whenever they have priority (and in certain other timing windows described by the mana rules) [605.3a][117.1d]. You still must be able to pay any activation costs (you can’t pay a cost unless you have the necessary resources) [118.3c]. Also, if an effect gives a player the option to pay mana during resolution, that player may activate mana abilities before doing so [608.2g].

results.question: [Counterspell] is on top of the stack targeting my [Divination]. When everyone passes priority, what resolves first, and does Divination still resolve?
results.text:
Counterspell resolves first, and Divination does not resolve because Counterspell’s effect counters (cancels) Divination and removes it from the stack. 

Why: When all players pass in succession, the top object on the stack resolves (rule [608.1]; see also [405.5] and [117.4]). Counterspell is the top spell, so Counterspell resolves first. When Counterspell resolves, its instruction (“Counter target spell”) is carried out; to “counter” a spell means to cancel it, removing it from the stack and putting it into its owner’s graveyard instead of allowing it to resolve (rule [701.6a]). Because Counterspell targeted Divination and Counterspell resolves first, Divination is countered and removed from the stack and therefore does not get to resolve. As a final part of resolving an instant or sorcery, that resolving spell is put into its owner’s graveyard (rule [608.2n]).

Definitions used: “Resolve” (in this answer) is when a spell’s instructions are followed and it has its effect, i.e., the controller follows the spell’s instructions in the order written while resolving an instant or sorcery (rule [608.2c]). “Counter” means to cancel the targeted spell so it doesn’t resolve and is put into its owner’s graveyard (rule [701.6a]).

Relevant cards: Counterspell is an instant that reads “Counter target spell.” Divination is a sorcery that reads “Draw two cards.” Because Divination was countered by Counterspell before Divination could resolve, Divination’s “Draw two cards” effect does not happen.

results.question: My [Charging Rhino] has trample and is blocked by [Vampire Nighthawk], which has deathtouch. How much combat damage do I have to assign to the blocker before I can trample the rest over to the player?
results.text:
You must assign 1 damage from Charging Rhino to Vampire Nighthawk, and the remaining 3 damage may be assigned to the defending player. Charging Rhino has power 4, so it assigns 4 combat damage total; because Vampire Nighthawk has deathtouch, any nonzero amount of damage assigned to Vampire Nighthawk is considered lethal for the purposes of assigning trample damage, so only 1 need be assigned to Vampire Nighthawk before excess can be assigned to the player.

Definitions and short reasoning: Trample is a keyword that modifies how an attacking creature assigns combat damage; the controller of an attacking creature with trample first assigns damage to the creature(s) blocking it and may assign excess to the player once all blocking creatures have been assigned lethal damage (rule 702.19b and 510.1a). Deathtouch means any nonzero amount of damage a source with deathtouch deals to a creature is considered lethal when determining excess damage for trample (rule 702.2c and Charging Rhino / Vampire Nighthawk card data). A creature’s power is the amount of combat damage it assigns (rule 510.1a and Charging Rhino’s 4 power), so Charging Rhino assigns 4 total: assign 1 to Vampire Nighthawk (that is lethal due to deathtouch) and the remaining 3 may be assigned to the defending player (per 702.19b and 120.4a).

results.question: I have [Monastery Swiftspear] on the battlefield and I cast [Shardless Agent]. When its cascade ability puts a noncreature spell onto the stack, does Monastery Swiftspear's prowess trigger before or after that cascaded spell resolves?
results.text:
Monastery Swiftspear's prowess will trigger when you cast the cascaded noncreature spell, and that prowess trigger will be put on the stack above the cascaded spell and resolve before the cascaded spell resolves.

Reasoning: Casting Shardless Agent causes its cascade trigger to resolve before Shardless Agent, and if you cast the exiled noncreature card you "cast" that spell as part of the cascade process (see Shardless Agent ruling #1 and rule 601.2i). A triggered ability that says "Whenever you cast a noncreature spell" (prowess) triggers when that cascaded spell is cast (see Prowess and Monastery Swiftspear ruling #1). Monastery Swiftspear's prowess trigger is placed on the stack on top of the spell that caused it to trigger and therefore resolves before that spell (Monastery Swiftspear ruling #2 and Monastery Swiftspear ruling #0).

Definitions relied on: "Triggered ability" — an ability with a trigger condition and an effect that goes on the stack when its condition happens (see rule 603.1). "To cast a spell" — to put it on the stack and pay its costs; abilities that trigger when a spell is cast trigger at that time (see rule 601.2i).

Assumption: You cast Shardless Agent and its cascade lets you cast a noncreature card. If instead the cascade didn't let you cast a spell, no prowess trigger would occur (Monastery Swiftspear ruling #1).

results.question: My opponent's [Grizzly Bears] has 2 damage marked on it. Do state-based actions make it die before my [Lightning Bolt] resolves?
results.text: Yes. If Grizzly Bears already has two damage marked on it before Lightning Bolt resolves, state-based actions will destroy Grizzly Bears before Lightning Bolt resolves. State-based actions are game actions that happen automatically whenever certain conditions are met; they don’t use the stack and are checked each time a player would receive priority, so a creature with damage marked equal to or greater than its toughness is destroyed as a state-based action before players receive priority and before the spell finishes resolving. Specifically, damage marked on Grizzly Bears equal to its toughness is lethal damage and causes it to be destroyed as a state-based action. The only relevant exception is if the two damage on Grizzly Bears is being created during the resolution of some other spell or ability that hasn’t finished resolving; state-based actions aren’t checked during the middle of a spell or ability’s resolution, so in that special timing the destruction might not happen until after that resolution finishes.

results.question: It's my upkeep. My [Phyrexian Arena]'s beginning-of-upkeep trigger and my opponent's own beginning-of-upkeep trigger both want to go on the stack. Who chooses the order, and when exactly do they trigger?
results.text:
Both triggered abilities trigger when the upkeep begins; when they’re put on the stack, you (the active player) put Phyrexian Arena’s triggered ability onto the stack first, then your opponent puts their beginning-of-upkeep triggered ability onto the stack, so your opponent’s ability will be the topmost object and will resolve first.

Reasoning and exact timing
- A “triggered ability” is an ability written like “At/When/Whenever [trigger event], [effect]” and has a trigger condition and an effect (definition: triggered ability) [603.1].
- When the upkeep step begins, abilities that trigger “at the beginning of” that step trigger (they automatically trigger at that moment) [500.6, 603.2b]. Phyrexian Arena’s text (“At the beginning of your upkeep, you draw a card and you lose 1 life.”) is such a triggered ability, so Phyrexian Arena’s ability triggers on your upkeep [Phyrexian Arena].
- The upkeep step has no turn-based actions, so there are no turn-based actions to handle before these triggers are considered; after triggers have been created, they are put onto the stack the next time a player would receive priority [503.1a, 117.3a].
- If multiple triggered abilities have triggered since the last time a player received priority, the game places them on the stack by having each player, in APNAP order, put all triggered abilities they control onto the stack in any order they choose (active player first, then nonactive players in turn order) [603.3b, 101.4]. That means on your upkeep you place Phyrexian Arena’s triggered ability onto the stack first, then your opponent places their triggered ability onto the stack on top of it, so the opponent’s ability resolves before Phyrexian Arena’s.

Multiplayer note: In a multiplayer game the same process applies — the active player’s triggered abilities are placed first, then each nonactive player in turn order places theirs [603.3b, 101.4, 805.7].

results.question: I cast a sorcery with buyback and pay its buyback cost, then copy that spell with [Fork]. Once everything resolves, how many copies of the card end up back in my hand?
results.text:
Only one card: the original sorcery (the spell you actually cast and paid buyback for) returns to your hand. The copy created by Fork does not put a card into your hand.

Why: "Buyback" means "If the buyback cost was paid, put this spell into its owner’s hand instead of into that player’s graveyard as it resolves" [702.27a]. The copy Fork creates is "a copy of [the] spell" that is put onto the stack and "is not cast" and has no card associated with it [707.10] and [Fork ruling #9]. Because the copy has no card to return, it can't produce a card returning to your hand; specifically, "If you copy a spell for which Buyback has been paid, you get nothing back since the copied spell does not have a card to give you" [Fork ruling #8]. Fork itself goes to the graveyard when it resolves and leaves only the copy on the stack (the copy still has no card) [Fork ruling #10].

Definitions: "Buyback" — the static ability that lets you pay an additional cost as you cast a spell and, if paid, causes that spell's card to be put into its owner's hand instead of its owner's graveyard as it resolves [702.27a]. "Copy of a spell" — a spell put onto the stack that copies the characteristics and decisions of another spell; a copy isn't cast and has no spell card associated with it [707.10].

results.question: I have a face-down manifested card that's really [Lightning Bolt]. It dies and I imprint it on [Mimic Vat]. Later I activate Mimic Vat's copy ability -- do I get a token?
results.text: No — you won't get a token. Mimic Vat may exile a manifested instant or sorcery card (such as Lightning Bolt), but you can’t create a token that’s a copy of a nonpermanent card, so Mimic Vat’s copy ability will not produce a token in this case.

results.question: My [Fiend Hunter]'s enters-the-battlefield ability is on the stack, about to exile a creature. I copy that ability with [Lithoform Engine] and target a second creature. Both get exiled. When Fiend Hunter later leaves the battlefield, do both come back?
results.text:
Yes. Both creatures exiled by Fiend Hunter’s enters-the-battlefield ability and the copy created by Lithoform Engine will return to the battlefield when Fiend Hunter leaves the battlefield.

Reasoning: Fiend Hunter has one ability that exiles a creature as it enters and a separate ability that returns “the exiled card” when Fiend Hunter leaves; those two abilities are linked (see rules 607.1 and 406.6). Lithoform Engine’s copy of Fiend Hunter’s enters-the-battlefield ability is also linked to Fiend Hunter’s leave-the-battlefield ability; copies of the first ability remain linked to the second (see Lithoform Engine ruling #4). When the phrase “the exiled card” is used but multiple cards were exiled (because the enter-the-battlefield ability was copied), that phrase refers to each of the exiled cards, so the return ability returns each of them (see rule 607.3).

Assumption/edge case: This answer assumes Fiend Hunter was on the battlefield when the exile abilities resolved and exiled both creatures. If Fiend Hunter left the battlefield before its first ability resolved, Fiend Hunter’s leave-the-battlefield ability would trigger and do nothing, and then the copied enter-the-battlefield ability could still exile a creature indefinitely (see Fiend Hunter ruling #0).

results.question: My own [Banishing Light] has an opponent's creature exiled. On my opponent's turn I cast [Teferi's Protection], phasing out my Banishing Light. Does the exiled creature return to the battlefield?
results.text:
No — the exiled creature stays exiled. Phasing Banishing Light does not cause its “until this leaves the battlefield” effect to end, so the creature does not return when Banishing Light phases out.

Reasoning: Banishing Light’s triggered ability exiled the creature “until this leaves the battlefield” (Banishing Light). Teferi's Protection causes all permanents you control, including Banishing Light, to phase out (Teferi's Protection). Phasing a permanent doesn’t make it leave the battlefield and zone-change abilities don’t trigger as a result of phasing (702.26d, 702.26c). In addition, the rules commentary for Teferi's Protection explicitly states that one-shot effects waiting “until [this] leaves the battlefield,” such as that of Banishing Light, won’t happen when a permanent phases out (Teferi's Protection ruling #21). While a permanent is phased out it’s treated as though it doesn’t exist (Teferi's Protection ruling #25), but that treatment isn’t the same as the permanent leaving the battlefield, so the exile condition remains in effect until Banishing Light actually leaves the battlefield.

Assumption: I assume the timing you described (you cast Teferi's Protection on your opponent’s turn and it resolves, phasing out Banishing Light immediately). If the timing were different (for example, Banishing Light left the battlefield for real before phasing), the result could differ because the exile ends when Banishing Light actually leaves the battlefield (Banishing Light).

results.question: I cast [Emrakul, the Promised End]. In response to its cast trigger, my opponent tries to [Counterspell] it. Can they even target it given protection from instants, and if it's countered, do I still control their next turn?
results.text:
Yes. Your opponent can target Emrakul, the Promised End with Counterspell while Emrakul, the Promised End is on the stack, and if Counterspell resolves and counters Emrakul, the triggered ability created when you cast Emrakul, the Promised End remains on the stack and can still cause you to gain control of the targeted opponent during that player's next turn (and give that player an extra turn afterward), assuming the triggered ability’s target is still legal when it resolves.

Why: “Protection” means a permanent or player can’t be targeted by spells with the stated quality (here, instants) while that permanent is on the battlefield [702.16b]. Emrakul, the Promised End’s protection from instants only applies while Emrakul, the Promised End is on the battlefield; Emrakul, the Promised End may be targeted by a spell that targets it while on the stack (for example, Syncopate) [Emrakul, the Promised End ruling #2]. Therefore Counterspell can target Emrakul, the Promised End while Emrakul, the Promised End is on the stack.

When you cast Emrakul, the Promised End its triggered ability (“When you cast this spell…”) is put on the stack and is a triggered ability that functions while that ability is on the stack [603.1a]. Triggered abilities on the stack aren’t spells and can’t be countered by things that counter only spells [113.9]. If Counterspell resolves and counters Emrakul, the Promised End, that doesn’t erase the already-created triggered ability; when that triggered ability later tries to resolve the game checks whether its target is still legal using last known information about its source if needed [608.2b]. If the triggered ability resolves successfully, you gain control of the targeted opponent during that player’s next turn and that player then takes an extra turn afterward; that is how a “control another player during that player’s next turn” effect functions (it applies to the next turn the affected player actually takes and lasts the entire turn) [723.1].

Assumption: I’m assuming your opponent cast Counterspell targeting the Emrakul, the Promised End spell on the stack in response to the cast and that no other effects (such as protection granted to the targeted opponent or other replacement/intervening effects) make the triggered ability’s target illegal. If the triggered ability’s target is illegal when the ability would resolve, the ability won’t have its effect [608.2b].

results.question: My cascade spell exiles cards until it hits [Valki, God of Lies], whose back face is the seven-mana planeswalker Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor. Is that a legal cascade hit, and can I cast the Tibalt side for free?
results.text:
Yes. Valki, God of Lies // Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor can be a legal cascade hit, because the card’s printed mana value is 2 and cascade stops when it exiles a nonland card whose mana value is less than the cascade spell’s mana value. You may be allowed to cast Valki, God of Lies // Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor from among the exiled cards with either face, but you may cast the Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor face without paying its mana cost only if the resulting spell’s mana value (Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor’s mana value is 7) is less than the cascade spell’s mana value; otherwise you cannot cast the Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor face via that cascade. 

Reasoning and definitions (rules quoted or paraphrased):
- Cascade: When you cast a spell with cascade, you exile cards from the top of your library until you exile a nonland card whose mana value is less than this spell’s mana value; you may cast that card without paying its mana cost if the resulting spell’s mana value is less than this spell’s mana value. [702.85a]
- The card in question, Valki, God of Lies // Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor, has a printed mana value of 2 (card data). Because cascade’s stop condition looks at the exiled card’s mana value, Valki, God of Lies // Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor is a legal card to stop on so long as your cascade spell’s mana value is greater than 2. [702.85a] (Valki, God of Lies // Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor (card data))
- Modal double-faced cards: if an effect allows you to play or cast a card from among a group of cards, you may play or cast a modal double-faced card with any face that fits the effect’s criteria. The criterion for cascade’s permission to cast without paying its mana cost is the “resulting spell’s mana value is less than this spell’s mana value” test, so you may choose the face only if that chosen face’s mana value satisfies that test. [Valki, God of Lies // Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor ruling #16][702.85a]
- When determining whether it’s legal to play/cast a particular face of a modal double-faced card, consider only the characteristics of the face you’re playing/casting. That means the “resulting spell’s mana value” in the cascade permission is the mana value of the chosen face (for Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor that is 7). [Valki, God of Lies // Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor ruling #14][712.11c]

Conclusion in practice: If your cascade spell’s mana value is greater than 2, it can hit Valki, God of Lies // Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor. You may choose to cast the Valki, God of Lies face (MV 2) or attempt to cast the Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor face (MV 7), but cascade only permits casting the chosen face without paying its mana cost if that chosen face’s mana value is less than the cascade spell’s mana value. Therefore, you cannot cast the Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor face for free unless your cascade spell’s mana value is greater than 7. If your cascade spell’s mana value is not greater than 7, the Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor face does not meet the cascade’s condition and cannot be cast via that cascade.
citations: Valki, God of Lies // Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor
Valki, God of Lies // Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor ruling #16
Valki, God of Lies // Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor ruling #14

results.question: I cast [Emrakul, the Promised End]. With its cast trigger on the stack, I copy that trigger with [Lithoform Engine]. Then I untap Lithoform Engine with [Voltaic Key] and use it again to copy [Emrakul, the Promised End] itself as a permanent spell. How many of my opponent's turns do I control, do I get a second Emrakul, and does copying the Emrakul spell give me another control-a-turn trigger?
results.text:
You will control exactly one of the targeted player’s turns (their next turn), you do get a second Emrakul, the Promised End as a token, and copying the Emrakul, the Promised End spell does not create another “When you cast this spell” trigger.

Reasoning and details:
- Copying the cast trigger: Lithoform Engine’s first ability can copy a triggered ability that’s on the stack and creates another instance of that ability on the stack (Lithoform Engine ruling #3). A copied triggered ability is the same ability (same source) as the original (Lithoform Engine ruling #0; see also rule 707.10b).
- Which control effect actually applies: Each resolved triggered ability from Emrakul, the Promised End would create a player-controlling effect for the targeted player’s next turn, but multiple player-controlling effects that affect the same player overwrite each other and the last one created is the one that actually controls that turn (Emrakul, the Promised End ruling #14). So although you have two such triggered-ability instances, only the one whose control effect was created last will determine who controls that next turn.
- Extra turns from each trigger: Each of those abilities also creates an extra turn for that player after that next turn. Each ability’s effect will create an extra turn (Emrakul, the Promised End ruling #14), and extra turns are added in the order they are created (the most recently created extra turn will be taken first) (rule 500.7). So both resolved triggers will produce extra turns for that player after the next turn.
- Copying the Emrakul, the Promised End spell itself: Lithoform Engine’s {4}, {T} ability copies a permanent spell on the stack and the copy is put onto the stack (see rule 707.10). Creating that copy won’t cause “when you cast this spell” abilities to trigger because the copy isn’t being cast (Lithoform Engine ruling #6; see rule 707.10). When the copy of a permanent spell resolves it becomes a token with the characteristics of the spell that became that token (rule 111.13). Therefore you get a second Emrakul, the Promised End as a token on the battlefield, but that token’s “When you cast this spell” trigger does not occur because the copy was not cast.

Assumption about timing: I assumed you copied the cast trigger while it was on the stack, so the two triggered abilities exist and will resolve in stack order; the one that resolves later is the one whose control effect is created last and therefore is the one that controls the targeted player’s next turn (see Lithoform Engine ruling #3 and Emrakul, the Promised End ruling #14). If the order in which the two triggers get created/resolved were different, the same overwrite rule (Emrakul, the Promised End ruling #14) would make the last-created control effect the one that applies.

results.question: I've imprinted a creature on [Mimic Vat] and activate its ability to make a token copy. While that ability is on the stack, I copy it with [Lithoform Engine]. Do I get two tokens?
results.text: Yes — you get two tokens, provided there is a card exiled with Mimic Vat when each instance of the ability resolves. Lithoform Engine’s ability copies the activated ability on the stack and puts another instance of that ability onto the stack ([Lithoform Engine ruling #3]). A copy of an ability is itself an ability and has the same source as the original ([707.10b]; see also [Lithoform Engine ruling #0]). Each resolving instance of Mimic Vat’s activated ability will create a token that’s a copy of whatever card is exiled with Mimic Vat at the time that instance resolves ([Mimic Vat ruling #4]). If no card is exiled with Mimic Vat when a given instance resolves, no token is created for that instance ([Mimic Vat ruling #6]).

results.question: An opponent controls an untapped [Trinisphere], and I have a permanent that makes my green spells cost {1} less. I want to cast [Awaken the Woods] for value. If I cast it with X=0, what does it cost and what do I get, and what X should I actually choose?
results.text:
Short answer: If you announce X = 0 when casting Awaken the Woods, the spell’s locked-in total mana cost will be {1}{G}{G} and it will create 0 1/1 green Forest Dryad land creature tokens. To get useful value you should announce X = 2 (that gives you two tokens) — X = 2, like X = 0 and X = 1, ends up costing {1}{G}{G}, but it creates two tokens instead of zero or one. 

Why (key definitions and the steps assumed):
- X: When you cast a spell with {X} in its mana cost, you choose and announce the value of X as part of casting the spell (definition from 107.3a and 601.2b). 
- Total cost: the mana cost (or alternative cost) plus any cost increases, minus any cost reductions; that resulting total cost is then locked in (see Total Cost and 601.2f). 

Step-by-step reasoning (casting with X announced as part of casting):
1) Announce X = 0 as part of casting Awaken the Woods ({X}{G}{G}) (107.3a; 601.2b). Awaken the Woods’s effect will create X 1/1 green Forest Dryad land creature tokens when it resolves (Awaken the Woods card data). 
2) Determine the spell’s mana cost before Trinisphere: with X = 0 the mana cost is {G}{G} (two green mana). Apply any cost reductions next (601.2f). A reduction that reduces generic mana doesn’t change colored symbols, so with no generic portion present the reduction does nothing; the cost is still {G}{G} (two mana) after reductions. 
3) Apply Trinisphere last (Trinisphere ruling #0): because the mana component after reductions is less than three, Trinisphere makes the spell cost three mana to cast while preserving the colored symbols. That turns {G}{G} into {1}{G}{G}. So the locked-in total cost you must pay is {1}{G}{G}. 
4) Resolution outcome: Awaken the Woods resolves and creates X = 0 tokens, i.e., zero 1/1 green Forest Dryad land creature tokens (Awaken the Woods card data). 

Which X should you choose instead? Brief calculations (same cost-determination steps as above):
- X = 0 → final cost {1}{G}{G} → 0 tokens. 
- X = 1 → start {1}{G}{G}; cost reduction removes 1 generic → {G}{G}; Trinisphere then raises it to {1}{G}{G} → final cost {1}{G}{G} → 1 token. 
- X = 2 → start {2}{G}{G}; cost reduction removes 1 generic → {1}{G}{G}; total is already three so Trinisphere does not change it → final cost {1}{G}{G} → 2 tokens. 
- X = 3 → start {3}{G}{G}; cost reduction removes 1 generic → {2}{G}{G} (total 4) → Trinisphere does not apply → final cost {2}{G}{G} → 3 tokens (but costs more). 

Therefore X = 2 is the cheapest X that gives you two tokens for the same locked-in cost {1}{G}{G}; it’s the best immediate “value” among small X choices. (If you want even more tokens, you can pick a higher X, but your locked-in cost will rise once X ≥ 3.)

Assumption about timing: I assumed normal timing for casting and locking in total cost (announce X while casting, then determine and lock the total cost). If you changed the announced X, the calculations above change accordingly (you must announce X as part of casting per 107.3a and 601.2b).

results.question: [Grist, the Hunger Tide] is in my graveyard. Can I return it with [Animate Dead], and what happens?
results.text:
Yes. You may target Grist, the Hunger Tide in your graveyard with Animate Dead; Animate Dead will return Grist, the Hunger Tide to the battlefield, but Animate Dead won’t be able to remain attached to Grist, the Hunger Tide on the battlefield, so Animate Dead will be put into its owner’s graveyard and its delayed triggered ability will cause Grist, the Hunger Tide to be sacrificed when that trigger resolves (if Grist, the Hunger Tide is still on the battlefield).

Why: Grist, the Hunger Tide is a creature card while it’s not on the battlefield, so it is a legal target for Animate Dead (see Grist, the Hunger Tide ruling #1). Animate Dead’s resolution returns the enchanted creature card to the battlefield and attempts to attach Animate Dead to that object (see Animate Dead ruling #1). Once Grist, the Hunger Tide is on the battlefield, Grist, the Hunger Tide is no longer a creature card and is only a planeswalker, so Animate Dead can’t legally be attached to Grist, the Hunger Tide; in that situation Animate Dead is put into its owner’s graveyard as a state-based action and the associated delayed triggered ability causes the returned permanent to be sacrificed when that trigger resolves (see Animate Dead ruling #4).

Definitions and assumptions:
- “Creature card in a graveyard” means a card that is a creature while it is in the graveyard; Grist, the Hunger Tide is such a card anywhere but on the battlefield (Grist, the Hunger Tide ruling #1). 
- I assume no other replacement effects or continuous effects change how Grist, the Hunger Tide enters the battlefield or would otherwise make Animate Dead able to legally enchant Grist, the Hunger Tide on the battlefield; if such effects exist the outcome could differ.

If you want the exact ruling text I relied on, see the citations below.

results.question: My commander [Skullbriar, the Walking Grave] has four +1/+1 counters on it. It dies, I move it to the command zone, then recast it. Does it keep the counters, and does [Doubling Season] double them as it re-enters?
results.text:
Yes. Skullbriar, the Walking Grave keeps its four +1/+1 counters when it’s moved to the command zone and those same four +1/+1 counters will be on Skullbriar, the Walking Grave as it enters the battlefield when you recast it; however, Doubling Season does not double those counters as Skullbriar, the Walking Grave enters.

Why: Skullbriar, the Walking Grave’s text and rulings make it an exception to the general “counters don’t move with objects” rule, so Skullbriar, the Walking Grave retains its counters as it changes zones other than a player’s hand or library (contrasting with the general rule that an object becomes a new object with no counters when it changes zones) [122.2], [400.7], Skullbriar, the Walking Grave, [Skullbriar, the Walking Grave ruling #3]. In a Commander game you may put Skullbriar, the Walking Grave into the command zone when it’s put into the graveyard or exile (so it ends up in the command zone with those counters) [903.9a].

Doubling Season does double counters that are put onto permanents as they enter the battlefield, but the counters that “remain on Skullbriar, the Walking Grave as it changes zones” are not considered to have been “placed” on it when it enters; the official ruling for Skullbriar, the Walking Grave explicitly says effects like Doubling Season won’t affect those counters [Skullbriar, the Walking Grave ruling #2], while Doubling Season’s rulings describe that it affects permanents that enter with counters (effects that put counters as they enter) (Doubling Season, [Doubling Season ruling #2]).

Definitions crucial to this ruling:
- “Counters that remain on Skullbriar, the Walking Grave as it changes zones”: counters that Skullbriar, the Walking Grave keeps because its card text says they remain when it leaves the battlefield to any zone other than a hand or library; those counters are not treated as having been placed on Skullbriar, the Walking Grave when it later enters a zone. See Skullbriar, the Walking Grave ruling #2. 
- “Enter with counters”: a permanent that “enters with counters” is one that has counters put on it as it enters the battlefield by some effect; Doubling Season affects those counters per its rulings (Doubling Season ruling #2). 

If you want a short timing note: this answer assumes Skullbriar, the Walking Grave was put into the command zone (via the Commander replacement/choice or SBA) before you recast it. If Skullbriar, the Walking Grave instead went to your hand or library at any point, its counters would not remain (Skullbriar, the Walking Grave’s exception excludes hand and library) [122.2], Skullbriar, the Walking Grave.

results.question: I cast [Final Fortune] to take an extra turn. During that extra turn I use [Sundial of the Infinite] to end the turn before the end step. Do I still lose the game?
results.text:
You do not lose the game. Sundial of the Infinite's ability ends the extra turn and skips that turn's end step, so Final Fortune's “At the beginning of that turn’s end step, you lose the game.” trigger never gets to trigger.

Reasoning and definitions (rules relied on are listed below):
- “End the turn” means performing an expedited process that skips nearly everything else that turn (see End the Turn). When an effect ends the turn, the current phase/step ends, creatures are removed from combat, the game skips straight to the cleanup step, and the end step is skipped (see [724.1d] and [End the Turn]).
- Because the end step is skipped by ending the turn this way, “at the beginning of the end step” triggered abilities don’t trigger that turn (see [724.1e] and Sundial of the Infinite ruling #1).
- Sundial of the Infinite ruling #4 explains that ending the turn this way exiles the stack, removes creatures from combat, checks state-based actions with no priority or triggered abilities put on the stack, then skips to the cleanup step; the end step is therefore not occurring that turn.
- Final Fortune gives you an extra turn and specifies that “At the beginning of that turn’s end step, you lose the game.” Because Sundial of the Infinite ends the extra turn before its end step and that end step is skipped, that “beginning of the end step” event never occurs and you do not lose the game (see Final Fortune ruling #1, which also confirms you don’t lose if the extra turn is skipped).

Therefore, activating Sundial of the Infinite during the extra turn created by Final Fortune so that the turn ends before the end step prevents the Final Fortune lose-the-game trigger, and you do not lose.

results.question: I cast [Clone]. When and how do I choose what it copies, and can my opponent respond to that choice?
results.text:
You choose what Clone copies as Clone is entering the battlefield — the choice is made by Clone’s controller while applying the replacement effect that makes Clone enter “as a copy.” That choice is part of the entering-the-battlefield event (not something put on the stack), so opponents do not get to respond to the choice itself after you make it. 

Reasoning and details:
- Clone’s ability is an “enter as a copy” effect, so Clone becomes a copy as it enters the battlefield and any “as this enters” choices are made for it as it enters (you make those choices for Clone) [707.5] [707.6].
- If multiple replacement effects would modify how Clone enters, the appropriate player chooses which replacement effect to apply as described by the replacement-effects rules; if any would cause Clone to enter as a copy, one of those must be chosen then [616.1c].
- Clone’s ability doesn’t target, and you may choose not to copy anything (in which case Clone enters as a 0/0 Shapeshifter) [Clone ruling #0] [Clone ruling #5].
- You may only choose a creature that’s already on the battlefield when you make the choice; you can’t choose a creature that’s entering at the same time as Clone [Clone ruling #2].
- If you choose a creature that itself is a copy of something else, Clone enters as whatever that creature copied (it becomes that copied object) [Clone ruling #4].

Assumption about timing: The answer assumes the normal case where Clone is resolving and is about to enter the battlefield; the choice is made during that resolution as part of applying the replacement effect. If you instead mean whether an opponent can respond while Clone is still a spell on the stack (i.e., before it resolves), they can of course cast spells or activate abilities in response to the Clone spell itself, but they cannot respond to the copy choice because that choice hasn’t been made until Clone is entering the battlefield (and the choice is not an event on the stack).

results.question: I activate my [Flooded Strand]'s ability, then activate [Gogo, Master of Mimicry] with X=2 to copy it twice. How many lands do I get from that one Flooded Strand?
results.text:
You get three lands total: the original Flooded Strand activation plus two additional instances created by Gogo, Master of Mimicry each let you search your library and put a Plains or Island onto the battlefield. 

Reasoning and definitions
- Copying an activated ability: To copy a spell, activated ability, or triggered ability means to put a copy of it onto the stack; a copy copies both the characteristics of the ability and all decisions made for it (including any additional costs paid) (707.10b). 
- What Gogo, Master of Mimicry does: Gogo, Master of Mimicry’s ability targets the activated ability on the stack and “creates one or more additional instances of that ability on the stack” (Gogo, Master of Mimicry ruling #6), and the copies have the same source as the original ability (Gogo, Master of Mimicry ruling #9). 
- Application to this interaction: You activated Flooded Strand’s ability first (so you paid its costs: {T}, 1 life, and sacrificed Flooded Strand). When you activate Gogo, Master of Mimicry with X=2 you put two copies of that activated Flooded Strand ability onto the stack in addition to the original instance that’s already on the stack (total of three instances). Each instance is an independent copy/instance that resolves separately and each instance’s effect is “Search your library for a Plains or Island card, put it onto the battlefield, then shuffle” (Flooded Strand). Because the effect doesn’t refer to the sacrificed Flooded Strand and copies copy the decisions/costs of the original as described above (707.10b), each of the three instances resolves and lets you put one land onto the battlefield. 

Assumption: This answer assumes Flooded Strand’s ability was activated and its costs were paid before Gogo, Master of Mimicry was activated (as you stated). If Flooded Strand hadn’t been activated and paid first, the interaction would be different because Gogo can only copy an activated ability that’s on the stack (Gogo, Master of Mimicry ruling #6).
